slides.title: Capillary blood: purpose and limits
bullets: Capillary sampling is the simplest method but error-prone; the main error is dilution of the blood with tissue fluid.

In adults and in children older than about 6 months blood is usually taken from a finger; in infants up to about 6 months from the medial or lateral surface of the heel; the back of the heel (close to bone) is avoided. The earlobe is used only rarely, in mass screening or research.
The international committee for standardisation in haematology and WHO recommend venous blood for ESR and for platelet counts (platelets stick to the edges of the puncture).

slides.title: Capillary blood: purpose and limits
bullets: Blood is usually taken in the morning, fasting, before exertion and diagnostic procedures.

slides.title: Materials
bullets: Sterile single-use lancets only — a new one for every puncture and every patient; cotton wool or gauze and 70% alcohol.
A pear-shaped plastic pipette to standardise the blood volume; if none is available, a small-bore single-use tube.
Rubber gloves and aseptic technique; the skin to be punctured should be dry and warm.
Lancets and finger-prick devices are never reused: reusable finger-prick devices have caused outbreaks of hepatitis B.

slides.title: Taking blood from a finger
bullets: 1. Use the third or fourth finger of the hand; do not use the index finger or the thumb.
2. Wipe the fingertip with cotton wool moistened with 70% alcohol and let it dry.
3. Puncture quickly and cleanly at the side of the fingertip with a sterile lancet (sensitivity is lower there).
4. Wipe away the first drop of blood with a cotton swab.

slides.title: Taking blood from a finger
bullets: 5. Squeeze the finger as gently as possible and collect the next drop with a plastic pipette.
6. After sampling, press firmly on the puncture site with a clean dry gauze or cotton-wool pad until the bleeding stops.

slides.title: Sources of error
bullets: Squeezing or crushing the finger mixes tissue fluid into the blood and spoils the result; the blood should flow freely from the wound.
If the finger is not squeezed and the first drop is wiped off, the error of dilution by tissue fluid can be avoided.
When several tests are taken from one puncture, the red-cell dilution is prepared first: the reagents for white cells and haemoglobin lyse red cells.

slides.title: Venous blood: tubes and requisition
bullets: Blood is taken strictly fasting, before any medication and before X-ray, endoscopic or ultrasound examinations.
EDTA tubes are for general clinical tests and glycated haemoglobin; sodium citrate for haemostasis tests; sodium fluoride for glucose; heparin for the immunogram and similar tests (not for PCR).
For serum (biochemical and immunoenzymatic tests) a dry tube without anticoagulant is used.
The requisition states the patient’s name, age, time of collection and the tests requested.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Treat all specimens as potentially infectious.
All work with the patient and biological material is done in rubber gloves; capillary blood is taken only with sterile material and a single-use scarifier.
With glass pipettes never aspirate material by mouth; use special rubber bulbs.
Do not use glassware with chipped edges; dispose of used lancets with the proper precautions.
